slides.cover: This talk presents MAQAC, a method for coordinating a fleet of drones that carry mobile base stations after a disaster. I will first show what existing methods miss, then what is new in MAQAC and why it is better, and then the simulation results, flight tests and demo videos that back this up.
slides.problem: After an earthquake or a flood, the cellular network is often the first thing to fail, and drones can bring it back. Three things make this hard. First, urgent users matter most. A first responder's session may not survive a long wait, so reaching people sooner is worth more than covering more area. Second, the drones coordinate over their own radio links, where messages are lost or late, and they may have to share one channel. Third, each drone only knows what its own detector sees. So the question is: can the drones coordinate from local information, with a guarantee that holds for the rule they actually run?
slides.idea: MAQAC works in rounds of one second. First, each drone shares short service records, saying which users were served and when. Second, it values every possible position from its own detections, those records, and a density prior, weighted by how urgent each user is. Third, it chooses the best footprint, with a soft partition of the area and a rule that keeps drones on the same channel apart. Then it flies there. In MAQAC, all drones choose at the same time, with no messages inside the round. In the variant MAQAC-S, the drones choose in turn, and each announces its choice once.
slides.events: The first result is about the objective. We describe each possible visit as a service event: which drone, which place, and the time it arrives. A user's value is its chance of still waiting at the earliest event that reaches it. Because the arrival time belongs to the event, the value no longer depends on the order in which drones choose. So the objective is submodular for any decreasing survival function, also when drones choose at the same time and their footprints overlap, and it equals the score we measure. Twenty thousand random checks found no violation.
slides.bound: The second result is a guarantee for every round, for the rule the drones actually run. It depends on three things. M is how many chosen footprints overlap on the same user, and it is measured after the round. Beta is how strongly drones are kept in their own region. And epsilon is the estimation error, which splits into a perception part and a backhaul delay part. In practice, overlaps were rare. In eighty-four to ninety percent of more than nine thousand measured rounds, no user was covered twice. The classical one half bound is only a special case, and we do not claim it.
slides.certificate: The third result is a certificate for each mission. Using a method called Learn then Test, we calibrate on past missions how much of the best achievable service a new mission will at least realise. On test missions, only two to three percent fell below the certified level, against an allowed ten percent. The certificate also decides where perception should run. Here, sending the camera frames to a larger model on the ground gave the higher certified share, so the certificate chose to offload.
slides.evaluation: We tested MAQAC at four levels. Nine thousand missions in a network level simulator. Ten thousand in a second, link limited model with realistic flight energy and larger areas. Forty-two missions in a city simulator, where every drone is flown by the PX4 flight control software. And thirty missions with a real Pixhawk flight controller in the loop, with all decisions computed on an embedded Jetson computer. The baselines include RAG, a recent distributed method from the IEEE Transactions on Robotics, two interference aware methods, a newer distributed method from IEEE TNSM, and MAPPO, a learned multi-agent policy.
slides.mainresult: Now the evidence. In the main simulator, MAQAC scores higher than the other distributed methods. Each bar shows how much higher MAQAC's score is. Against RAG, the strongest rival, MAQAC is four to seven percent higher in urban and suburban fleets of four to ten drones, where several drones compete for spread-out users, and level in the other configurations. The ties have simple reasons. Two drones rarely compete for the same users, and in the disaster scenario all users sit in a few tight clusters that both methods find. MAQAC is also seven to thirteen percent ahead of the interference aware methods, and eight to thirteen percent ahead of the learned MAPPO policy in urban and suburban areas.
slides.losswins: The second model shows where record sharing pays off. RAG reaches each decision through several rounds of messages. When messages are lost, two drones can miss each other's commitments and go after the same users. MAQAC-S sends only one announcement per drone. With forty percent of messages lost, MAQAC-S scored three to twenty-two percent higher than RAG in every configuration on three kilometre areas. When the whole fleet shares one channel, it was up to nine percent ahead. And on a reliable network, it reaches the same score with five to eight times fewer coordination messages.
slides.flight: Next, real flight control. In the city simulator, every drone was flown by its own PX4 flight stack, and had to climb over towers up to two hundred and thirty-seven metres tall. Real flight changed the score by less than five percent. In forty-two missions, the simulator recorded no collision in flight: no two drones came closer than twenty metres, and none came closer than nineteen metres to a building. In thirty more missions, a real Pixhawk flight controller flew one drone, while a Jetson computer made all the fleet's decisions in seventeen to thirty-three milliseconds per round.
slides.takeaways: To sum up. MAQAC is better: it serves four to seven percent more urgent sessions than RAG, and eight to thirteen percent more than MAPPO, because it values waiting time. It is robust: up to twenty-two percent ahead of RAG when messages are lost, with five to eight times fewer messages, because it shares records instead of negotiating. It is certifiable: its bound holds for the rule actually run, and its mission certificate held in all twenty flown missions. And it is real: flight with PX4 and a Pixhawk in the loop changed the score by less than five percent, with decisions in under thirty-five milliseconds on a Jetson. The code, the results and these videos are in the project repository. Thank you.
slides.sota: Several kinds of methods address parts of this problem. Distributed submodular methods, such as RAG from the IEEE Transactions on Robotics, come with guarantees, but they negotiate over several rounds of messages and assume exact information, so neither perception error nor message delay enters their bound. Multi-agent reinforcement learning, such as MAPPO, can value urgent users, but it gives no guarantee. Deployment methods with guarantees assume that the users are known, and formulations that value waiting time assume a fixed service order. Conformal methods calibrate perception, but do not certify the coordination itself. No existing method has all five properties. MAQAC is designed to have all of them.
slides.novelty: MAQAC brings three ideas. First, it values each user by how long the user has waited, through time-stamped service events, so urgency can be optimised even when all drones choose at once. This is why it serves more urgent sessions: four to seven percent more than RAG, and seven to thirteen percent more than interference aware methods, which ignore waiting time. Second, the drones share short records of who was served, instead of negotiating their choices. A lost message therefore costs little, which is why MAQAC-S stays up to twenty-two percent ahead of RAG when forty percent of messages are lost, while sending five to eight times fewer messages. Third, MAQAC comes with a guarantee for the rule the drones actually run, and with a certificate for each mission, so an operator knows the service level in advance. The certificate held in more than ninety-seven percent of test missions, and in all twenty flown missions. The rest of this talk shows how the method works, and then the evidence.

The circles are the drones' coverage footprints, and on the right is each method's running score. MAQAC and MAQAC-S spread their drones across the area, and finish with the highest scores.
